'''Owaribe Shrine''' (尾張戸神社, ''Owaribe Jinja'') is a {{ill|Shinto shrine|en|Shinto shrine|qid=Q845945|lt=Shinto shrine|1=Shinto shrine}} located in {{ill|Nagoya|en|Nagoya|qid=Q11751|lt=Nagoya|1=Nagoya}}'s {{ill|Moriyama-ku, Nagoya|en|Moriyama-ku, Nagoya|qid=Q1155291|lt=Moriyama Ward|1=Moriyama-ku, Nagoya}} and {{ill|Seto, Aichi|en|Seto, Aichi|qid=Q499493|lt=Seto City|1=Seto, Aichi}}, {{ill|Aichi Prefecture|en|Aichi Prefecture|qid=Q80434|lt=Aichi Prefecture|1=Aichi Prefecture}}. It is a {{ill|Engishiki Jinmyōchō|1=Engishiki Jinmyōchō|2=ja|3=延喜式神名帳|4=zh|5=延喜式神名帳|6=simple|7=Engishiki Jinmyōchō|ja|延喜式神名帳|lt=Shikinaisha}} and formerly held the Rank of [[Gōsha]].
The shrine is situated atop [[Tōgokusan]], a mountain also known by other names such as "Oku-no-in of Atsuta" and "Tōgoku Myōjin."
== Enshrined deities ==
The shrine enshrines the following three deities:<ref>Shrine history and explanatory plaque.</ref><ref group="note">According to ''Nihon no Kamigami,'' the shrine also enshrines [[Otoyo-no-Mikoto]] and [[Amato Hime-no-Mikoto]].</ref> These deities are ancestors of the [[Owari clan]].
* '''[[Amenohoakari-no-Mikoto]]'''
*: Ancestral deity of the Owari clan.
* '''[[Amenokaguyama-no-Mikoto]]'''
*: Also known as [[Takakuraji-no-Mikoto]]. Eldest son of Amenohoakari-no-Mikoto.
* '''[[Takeinadane-no-Mikoto]]'''
*: Twelfth-generation descendant of Amenohoakari-no-Mikoto.
According to legend, Amenokaguyama-no-Mikoto (Takakuraji-no-Mikoto) descended on [[Takakurayama]], across the [[:en:Shonai River|Shonai River]], before relocating to Tōgokusan.<ref name="shrinehistory">Shrine history and explanatory plaque.</ref> He is said to have crossed the river riding a white deer, which is commemorated in the name of "Kanou Bridge" (鹿乗橋).
== History ==
=== Foundation ===
According to shrine tradition, recorded in the "Tōgokusan Daimyōjin Sōsō Honki," the shrine was founded in the 5th year of the reign of Emperor [[:en:Seimu|Seimu]] by [[Miyazu-hime-no-Mikoto]], a consort of {{ill|Yamato Takeru|en|Yamato Takeru|qid=Q461258|lt=Yamato Takeru|1=Yamato Takeru}} and sister of Takeinadane-no-Mikoto.<ref name="shrinehistory" />
The late Edo-period geographical work ''[[:en:Owari Meisho Zue|Owari Meisho Zue]]'' explains that Tōgokusan was originally called "Owariyama" because the Owaribe gods were enshrined there. Over time, "Owari" became "Tōkoku" (a reference to Owari Province), and eventually, the name evolved into "Tōgokusan."
The shrine stands atop a Kofun known as "Owaribe Shrine Kofun," part of the [[Shidami Kofun group|Shidami Kofun Group]]. These mounds are traditionally attributed to members of the [[Owari clan]]. The shrine's name "Owaribe" is thought to derive from "Owari-be," indicating followers or subjects of the Owari clan.
=== Later history ===
The shrine is listed in the ''[[Engishiki]]'' (927 CE) as a minor {{ill|Engishiki Jinmyōchō|1=Engishiki Jinmyōchō|2=ja|3=延喜式神名帳|4=zh|5=延喜式神名帳|6=simple|7=Engishiki Jinmyōchō|ja|延喜式神名帳|lt=Shikinaisha}} under the name "Owaribe Shrine."<ref name="place-names">''Aichi Prefecture Place names,'' entry for Owaribe Shrine.</ref> By the late Heian period, it was recorded as "Owaribe Tenjin" in the ''Owari Province Divine names List.''<ref name="place-names" />
During the {{ill|Edo period|en|Edo period|qid=Q184963|lt=Edo period|1=Edo period}}, the [[Tokugawa clan]] became patrons of the shrine, seeing it as an important spiritual site near the [[Kimon]] (northeast direction) of [[Nagoya Castle]]. In 1665, the second lord of [[Owari Domain]], {{ill|Tokugawa Mitsutomo|en|Tokugawa Mitsutomo|qid=Q843245|lt=Tokugawa Mitsutomo|1=Tokugawa Mitsutomo}}, ordered the construction of the Chūsha and Minami-sha subordinate shrines, along with a Yakushidō (medicine hall). These structures were rebuilt and maintained under the Tokugawa family's auspices.<ref name="shrinehistory" />
Following the [[Meiji Restoration]], the shrine was designated a [[Gōsha]] in 1872 under the [[modern shrine Ranking system]].
== Main building ==
The main hall of the shrine, originally built in {{ill|Hachiman-zukuri|en|Hachiman-zukuri|qid=Q3125455|lt=Hachiman-zukuri|1=Hachiman-zukuri}} style, was rebuilt in [[Shinmei-zukuri]] style during the {{ill|Meiji era|en|Meiji era|qid=Q3125096|lt=Meiji era|1=Meiji era}}.<ref>''Kamishidami Historical Records,'' p. 115.</ref>
A small shrine known as the "Mikuro Myōjin" is located on the northwest slope. This was constructed to enshrine a rediscovered medieval jar burial during pathway construction in 1935.<ref>''Shidami Historical Records,'' pp. 31, 44.</ref>
